theory.intro: **Volume** is the amount of space an object takes up. **Capacity** is the amount a container can hold. Volume uses cubic units and capacity uses litre units, and the best unit is the one giving a number that is easy to picture.
facts: $\text{mm}^3$ (cubic millimetres) suit tiny solids: a bead, a grain of sand, a pin head.
$\text{cm}^3$ (cubic centimetres) suit small solids: a sugar cube, an eraser, a matchbox.
$\text{m}^3$ (cubic metres) suit large solids and spaces: a load of soil, a fridge, a shipping container.
**Millilitres (mL)** suit small amounts of liquid: a teaspoon, a dose of medicine, a can of drink.
**Litres (L)**, each $1000$ mL, suit everyday amounts: a milk bottle, a bucket, a fuel tank.
**Kilolitres (kL)**, each $1000$ L, suit large amounts: a rainwater tank, a backyard pool.
**Megalitres (ML)**, each $1000$ kL, suit very large amounts: a dam, a reservoir, a town's water supply.
A solid block of wood has volume but no capacity, since it cannot hold anything inside; a bottle has both.
$1\text{ cm}^3$ of space holds exactly $1$ mL, $1000\text{ cm}^3$ holds $1$ L, and $1\text{ m}^3$ holds $1$ kL.
The best unit gives a number neither enormous nor far below $1$: a bathtub reads better as $250$ L than $250\,000$ mL.
steps: Decide whether you are measuring space taken up (volume) or amount held (capacity).
Compare the size with a benchmark: a bead, a sugar cube, a truck load; a teaspoon, a bucket, a pool, a dam.
Choose the unit that gives a number that is easy to say and write.

foundation.question_text: Does a solid house brick have a volume, a capacity, or both? Explain your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
A brick takes up space on the ground, so it has a volume.
It is solid all the way through, so nothing can be poured into it.
A volume only.

foundation.question_text: Does an empty plastic drink bottle have a volume, a capacity, or both? Explain your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
The bottle takes up space on a shelf, so it has a volume.
It is hollow and can be filled with liquid, so it also has a capacity.
Both.

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the volume of a single bead: $\text{mm}^3$, $\text{cm}^3$ or $\text{m}^3$?
foundation.solution_text:
A bead is only a few millimetres across in every direction.
A cube of side $1$ mm is the cube that matches a solid that small.
$\text{mm}^3$

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the volume of a sugar cube: $\text{mm}^3$, $\text{cm}^3$ or $\text{m}^3$?
foundation.solution_text:
A sugar cube is about a centimetre along each edge.
A cube of side $1$ cm matches it almost exactly.
$\text{cm}^3$

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the volume of soil in a truck load: $\text{mm}^3$, $\text{cm}^3$ or $\text{m}^3$?
foundation.solution_text:
A truck load of soil is metres across in every direction.
A cube of side $1$ m is the cube that matches a load that big.
$\text{m}^3$

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the capacity of a teaspoon of cough medicine: mL, L, kL or ML?
foundation.solution_text:
A teaspoon holds only a few drops.
The millilitre is the smallest unit on the capacity ladder and matches a dose that size.
mL

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the capacity of a bucket of water: mL, L, kL or ML?
foundation.solution_text:
A bucket holds far more than a teaspoon but nothing like a swimming pool.
The litre is the everyday unit for amounts a person can carry.
L

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the capacity of a backyard swimming pool: mL, L, kL or ML?
foundation.solution_text:
A pool holds thousands of litres, so litres would give a five-digit count.
The kilolitre is a thousand litres and keeps the number short.
kL

foundation.question_text: Which unit is most appropriate for the water stored behind a country town's dam: mL, L, kL or ML?
foundation.solution_text:
A dam holds enough water to supply a whole town, far more than a thousand kilolitres.
The megalitre is the largest unit on the capacity ladder and is the one water authorities use.
ML

foundation.question_text: Write the abbreviations for a kilolitre and a megalitre, and state how many kilolitres make one megalitre.
foundation.solution_text:
A kilolitre is written kL and a megalitre is written ML.
Each step up the capacity ladder is a thousand times larger.
kL and ML, and $1000$ kL make $1$ ML.

foundation.question_text: A container has a volume of $1\text{ cm}^3$. What capacity, in millilitres, will exactly fill it?
foundation.solution_text:
A cubic centimetre of space holds exactly one millilitre.
$1$ mL

development.question_text: Which of these is most likely to have a capacity of about $5$ mL: a teaspoon of vanilla, a kettle of water or a backyard pool?
development.solution_text:
A millilitre is about the size of a large drop, so $5$ mL is only a few drops.
A kettle holds litres and a pool holds kilolitres.
A teaspoon of vanilla.

development.question_text: Which of these is most likely to have a capacity of about $200$ L: a kitchen sink, a household hot-water tank or a farm dam?
development.solution_text:
$200$ L is about the amount that fills a large wheelie bin.
A kitchen sink holds only a few litres and a farm dam holds megalitres.
A household hot-water tank.

development.question_text: Nadia records the medicine in a bottle as $0.000015$ kL. Her measurement is correct. Explain why kL is not the most appropriate unit here, and state a better one.
development.solution_text:
A kilolitre is a thousand litres, far more than a medicine bottle holds, so the reading comes out as a decimal with four leading zeros.
A bottle of medicine holds only a few spoonfuls, so the millilitre matches it.
mL

development.question_text: A water authority records the water in a reservoir as $4\,500\,000\,000$ mL. Explain why mL is not the most appropriate unit here, and state a better one.
development.solution_text:
A millilitre is about a drop, so counting a reservoir in millilitres runs to ten digits and cannot be pictured.
A reservoir holds the supply of a whole town, so the megalitre matches it.
ML

development.question_text: Ravi records the volume of his pencil case as $0.0015\text{ m}^3$. Explain why $\text{m}^3$ is not the most appropriate unit here, and state a better one.
development.solution_text:
A cubic metre is a cube a metre along each edge, far bigger than a pencil case, so the reading sits well below $1$.
A pencil case is a few centimetres each way, so the cubic centimetre matches it.
$\text{cm}^3$

development.question_text: Put these units of capacity in order from smallest to largest: kL, mL, ML, L.
development.solution_text:
Each step up the ladder is $1000$ times the one below it.
The millilitre is the smallest and the megalitre is the largest.
mL, L, kL, ML

development.question_text: Put these units of volume in order from largest to smallest: $\text{cm}^3$, $\text{m}^3$, $\text{mm}^3$.
development.solution_text:
The cubes are built on edges of $1$ mm, $1$ cm and $1$ m.
Ordering the edges orders the cubes.
$\text{m}^3$, $\text{cm}^3$, $\text{mm}^3$

development.question_text: A sealed tank has a volume of $1\text{ m}^3$. State its capacity in kilolitres, and then in litres.
development.solution_text:
A cubic metre of space holds exactly one kilolitre.
A kilolitre is a thousand litres.
$1$ kL, which is $1000$ L

development.question_text: A house brick and a bucket take up about the same amount of space. Explain which of the two has a capacity, and which has only a volume.
development.solution_text:
Both take up space, so both have a volume.
The brick is solid, so nothing can be poured into it and it has no capacity.
The bucket is hollow, so it has a capacity as well as a volume.

mastery.question_text: A display board records the size of four things: a grain of rice, a dose of eye drops, the concrete poured for a driveway, and the water held by a town reservoir. Choose the most appropriate unit for each, and state the rule you used to decide.
mastery.solution_text:
A grain of rice is a solid a few millimetres long: $\text{mm}^3$.
Eye drops are a liquid and a dose is only a few drops: mL.
Concrete for a driveway is a solid load metres across: $\text{m}^3$.
A town reservoir holds far more than a thousand kilolitres: ML.
The rule is to use cubic units for the space a solid takes up and litre units for what a container holds, then pick the size closest to the thing being measured.

mastery.question_text: A water utility wants a single unit used in every row of its report, from the water wasted by a dripping tap to the water in the city's whole supply. Explain the two problems this creates, and name the unit you would use for each of those two rows if the rule were dropped.
mastery.solution_text:
If the shared unit is small, such as mL, the city's supply becomes a number with twelve digits that nobody can picture.
If the shared unit is large, such as ML, a dripping tap becomes a decimal with several leading zeros and rounds away to nothing.
No single unit sits close to both sizes, so one row is always unreadable.
A dripping tap suits mL and the city's supply suits ML.

mastery.question_text: A school's rainwater tank can be recorded as $22\,000$ L, $22$ kL or $0.022$ ML, and all three are correct. Which would a tank supplier's catalogue use, and why?
mastery.solution_text:
$0.022$ ML is a decimal well below $1$, so the size is hard to picture.
$22\,000$ L is a five-digit count, which is accurate but clumsy to compare between models.
$22$ kL is a short whole number, and kilolitres are the unit tank suppliers already use.
$22$ kL
